content: Brine is a solution of water that is either saturated or nearly saturated with sodium chloride (NaCl). Historically, it has been widely used for the preservation of vegetables, fish, and meat, although its popularity for this purpose has declined over time. Brine is also commonly employed in the aging process of cheeses such as Halloumi and Feta. While brine shares preservation properties with substances like sugar or vinegar, it has additional applications, particularly in the transportation of heat. The addition of salt to water lowers the freezing point of the solution, making it an efficient and cost-effective medium for heat transfer. For example, at a salt concentration of 23.3%, the freezing point of brine is reduced to -21°C (-6°F). At 15.5°C (60°F), saturated brine contains 26.4% salt by weight, while at 0°C (32°F), it can hold up to 23.3% salt. Brine has several other applications beyond preservation. It is used to pre-treat roads before winter storms by being poured onto roadways alongside salt pellets. This combination lowers the freezing point of surface water, causing snow and ice to melt at higher temperatures, thereby improving road safety. In ice rinks, such as those used for hockey or figure skating, brine is circulated through refrigeration systems and returned beneath the ice slab at a colder temperature to maintain the ice surface. Brine is also utilized in the cooling systems of cruise ships and as a quenching medium for cooling ferrous metals during industrial processes. In Europe, brine baths are sometimes employed for medicinal purposes, treating conditions such as skin disorders and bladder issues. In the offshore oil and gas industry, brine is used in combination with monoethylene glycol (MEG) to flood pipelines before commissioning. This prevents the formation of hydrates during production start-up, depending on the specific properties of the well. In Arctic regions, where the ground is permanently frozen (permafrost), brine is used in underground mining to enable the use of water-fed drills without freezing. Additionally, chilled brine can be employed to locally freeze the water table, allowing mine shafts to be constructed without the risk of flooding. In chemical processes, brine is frequently used to dry organic solvents after an aqueous wash. The brine wash removes most of the water from the organic solvent, with any remaining water typically removed using chemical drying agents such as anhydrous magnesium sulfate. Brine plays a critical role in the chloralkali process, where it is electrolyzed to produce sodium hydroxide, chlorine gas, and hydrogen gas on an industrial scale. During this process, chloride ions are oxidized to chlorine gas, while water is reduced to hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions. The hydroxide ions combine with sodium ions to form sodium hydroxide upon evaporation. By modifying the reaction conditions, the chlorine gas can also react with hydroxide ions to produce hypochlorite and chlorate salts. Brine is further utilized in the Solvay process to manufacture sodium carbonate and in the solution mining of salt from underground deposits. In the pharmaceutical industry, brine is used in various applications. When employed for industrial purposes, brine is typically transported through pipelines made of welded steel, which are coated to protect against corrosion.
